name: Socrates
quote: The unexamined life is not worth living.
script: I am Socrates. Athens put me on trial for asking too many questions. Some said I should simply keep quiet. I told them: The unexamined life is not worth living. Swipe and I will show you how to examine yours.

morning_slides.title: A life you never question isn’t fully yours.
body: Most of what we believe, want and fear was handed to us: by parents, friends, ads, habit. Socrates thought a good life starts when you stop running on those defaults and ask why.
At his trial he said that talking every day about how to live well was the greatest good a person could have. He would rather die than stop asking.

morning_slides.title: Who was Socrates?
body: An Athenian philosopher who spent his life questioning people in the marketplace. He wrote nothing; we know him mostly through his student Plato.
In 399 BC, at about 70, he was tried for impiety and corrupting the young, and sentenced to death. Plato’s Apology records his defense.

morning_slides.title: Tonight, pick one belief or habit and ask:
steps: Why do I believe this? Where did it come from?
What would change if I were wrong?
Knowing what I know now, would I still choose it?

morning_slides.title: What’s one belief you’ve never questioned?
morning_slides.body: Tell us below. The best answers start a real conversation.

evening_slides.text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
“Know thyself” was carved at the temple of Apollo at Delphi. Socrates made it a way of life.
Every answer you examine becomes your own.
Tonight’s question: what did you do today only because you’ve always done it?

caption_morning_fb:
Are you living on autopilot?

At his trial in Athens in 399 BC, Socrates refused to stop questioning people, even to save his life. He told the jury: “The unexamined life is not worth living.” (Plato, Apology 38a)

What he meant: much of what we believe and want was handed to us by habit and the people around us. A good life starts when we ask why.

Tonight, pick one belief or habit and ask:
1. Why do I believe this? Where did it come from?
2. What would change if I were wrong?
3. Knowing what I know now, would I still choose it?

What’s one belief you’ve never questioned? Tell us in the comments.
